label: Hot surfaces
summary: Exhaust pipes, engines, motors that have been running, heating elements, soldering irons, heat sinks, lamps, freshly cut or ground metal and discharge resistors can be hot enough to burn skin in a second. Burns infect easily, and without care large burns kill.
signs: Shimmering air, discolouration, or a hot smell
Blue or straw-coloured metal after grinding or welding
Glowing elements, or elements that look normal but were just switched off
do: Let things cool before handling them
Hold the back of your hand near a part, without touching, to feel for heat
Put hot tools on a stand, never on the bench or the ground
Hold small parts with pliers while cutting, grinding or soldering
Keep a container of clean water near hot work

An IR thermometer reads shiny bare metal far too low: a stainless pot of boiling water can read about 38 °C (100 °F). Read a strip of electrical tape or flat paint on the part instead, or treat it as hot
A heated seat for someone with poor feeling: lowest level only (Dometic's rule for people with impaired heat sensitivity). Sunbeam says not to use its blankets and pads with them at all
Keep blankets, coats and bedding off a heated seat or an electric blanket while it is switched on: Dometic and UL both say so, and UL says heat gets trapped in the layers
dont: Don't grab metal you have just cut, ground, drilled or welded
Don't touch elements, bulbs or exhausts to see if they're hot
Don't open radiator or coolant caps on a hot engine
Don't wear synthetic clothes for hot work: they melt onto skin

Don't use heating pads, electric blankets or heated seats on anyone who can't feel heat or move away from it: babies and young children, anyone paralysed, diabetics, people with poor circulation, or anyone incapacitated or immobile (a very drunk or heavily sedated person may be)
A paraplegic driver got a deep hip burn from 30 minutes on a seat heater set to high
ppe: Untreated cotton long sleeves; synthetics melt onto skin
firstAid: Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20; don't use ice
Take off rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts, but leave anything that is stuck to the burn
Cover loosely with clean plastic film or a clean non-fluffy cloth
Don't pop blisters or put butter, oil or toothpaste on a burn
Burns wider than about 5–8 cm (2–3 in), deep, white or charred burns, burns on the face, hands, feet, joints or groin, and any burn on a child need medical care
Keep the rest of the person warm while you cool the burn; large burns and small children chill quickly
